description: We are winning with this one
summary:
We developed MANGO (MANGO Ain’t No Greenwash Observer), an app that shows the history of any mangrove area in minutes. The user draws a box of up to 25 km² on the coast and picks a date range. MANGO then analyzes more than 40 years of NASA/USGS Landsat imagery together with daily NASA POWER climate data. It reports whether the mangrove was conserved, suffered a structural loss (with the date, the hectares lost, and what replaced it), or was never there.

MANGO uses NASA’s open data to answer the challenge of monitoring coastal ecosystems and how they respond to climate. It separates permanent loss of extent from temporary canopy stress, such as droughts or hurricanes the forest recovers from. It also matches each change against internationally defined climate extremes, so users can tell when weather explains a loss and when it points to human activity. Every threshold comes from published standards or the site’s own data.

Mangroves store large amounts of carbon, protect coasts from storms, and support fisheries, yet they keep disappearing. MANGO is free, needs no account, and runs with one click. Authorities, communities, and carbon projects can use it to check whether a conservation claim is real or greenwashing.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

MANGO tells you what has happened to any mangrove area over the last 40 years. The user picks a date range and draws a box of up to 25 km² on a map. The backend then downloads the full Landsat 5/7/8/9 archive for that box (1984 to the present) from Microsoft Planetary Computer, along with daily NASA POWER climate data since 1981.

It removes clouds in four layers:

Landsat’s official quality mask

a thermal test

a temporal spike filter

requiring two clean observations before a pixel counts as lost

Next, MANGO maps the mangrove using a baseline from the earliest years. It detects structural breaks with the PELT algorithm and accepts a loss only if it persists for 12–18 months. Finally, it compares each change against climate extremes defined by international standards (ETCCDI and WMO): extreme rainfall, strong wind, drought (SPI-3) and heatwaves. The result is one of three outcomes: conserved, structural loss (with date, hectares and new land cover), or no mangrove present.

What benefits does it have?

Results in minutes, with no remote-sensing expertise needed

Free, no accounts, runs locally with one click

Transparent: every threshold comes from a published standard or the site’s own data

Tells permanent loss apart from temporary stress such as drought or a hurricane the forest recovers from

Local caching makes repeat queries fast

What is the intended impact?

Mangroves store large amounts of carbon, protect coasts from storms and support fisheries. MANGO makes their monitoring cheaper and easier to access. Environmental authorities can verify deforestation reports. Blue-carbon projects can check that protected areas are still standing. Communities and journalists can tell whether a conservation claim is real or greenwashing.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

Python, with FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio and pystac-client

JavaScript, with React, Vite and Leaflet

Data: NASA POWER, Landsat Collection 2 Level 2 via the STAC catalog of Microsoft Planetary Computer, and Global Mangrove Watch v4.1

pytest (88 automated tests), ruff and Git/GitHub

Ordinary laptops running Windows; no special hardware

How is your project creative?

Most tools show only a “before and after” map. MANGO gives the month of the change, separates the area lost from the health of the remaining forest, and links each change to climate events. When no extreme event explains a loss, that points to human activity. The name is a recursive acronym that states the goal: holding greenwashing accountable with satellite evidence.

What factors did your team consider?

Scientific rigor: standard definitions, robust statistics, no invented thresholds

Honesty about uncertainty: months without data appear as gaps, results from the last 18 months are marked provisional, and coincidence with an event is never presented as proof of cause

Known limitations: clouds, tides, climate data at ~50 km resolution, and the 30 m pixel size

Validation: synthetic scenarios, a real case in Mandinga (Veracruz), and comparison with Global Mangrove Watch

Accessibility and cost: free, local and simple to use

Scalability: the API is separate from the frontend, so it can move to a server later
